The disconnect between oil stocks and the broader market has rarely been wider:

The 6-month correlation between the S&P 500 Energy Sector and the S&P 500 is down to -0.38, near its lowest on record.

This marks a sharp reversal from a positive correlation of +0.74 observed in June 2025.

In the last week of September, this figure fell as low as -0.45, the lowest reading in data going back to the 1980s.

The only other time since the late 1980s when the correlation between these two indices turned negative was in 2000 and 2001, during the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

This all comes as the S&P 500 Energy Sector has rallied +23.1% over the last 6 months, significantly outperforming the S&P 500’s gain of +7.1%.

Energy stocks are having a historic year amid the Iran War.

BREAKING: The Consumer Confidence Index surged +7.5 points in October, to 91.7, its highest since May 2026.

This marks its largest monthly increase since May 2025.

The Present Situation Index jumped +8.6 points, to 120.4, its highest since April.

At the same time, the Expectations Index rose +6.9 points, to 72.6, nearly reversing 3 consecutive monthly declines.

The increase in sentiment was largely driven by the recent decline in retail gasoline prices, which provided some relief to household budgets.

Furthermore, consumers reported improved perceptions of the job market and business conditions.

Consumer confidence remains highly volatile.

It's officially Fed day.

We expect a "hawkish pause" today.

The Fed will hold interest rates unchanged but lay the groundwork for a December rate hike, bringing total rate hikes in 2026 to +50 basis points.

Why?

Because the US economy is now facing both supply-side and rising demand-side inflationary pressures, while the labor market continues to weaken beneath the surface.

This puts the Fed in an increasingly difficult position: Inflation is demanding tighter monetary policy, while underlying labor market weakness is calling for the opposite.

We expect the Fed to prioritize inflation today, keeping the door open for further tightening in December.

The relationship between stocks and bonds has flipped again:

The 20-day correlation between the 10Y Note Yield and the Nasdaq 100 is up to +0.51, its highest since the March pullback.

This marks a sharp reversal from the negative correlation of -0.68 recorded in the last week of September.

This also follows 6 consecutive months in which the 20-day correlation between the two assets remained negative.

This comes as Treasuries once again acted as a hedge against the drop in tech stocks, as they did during the March pullback and the March-April 2025 correction.

To put this into perspective, during the 2020 pandemic crash, the 20-day correlation between the 10Y Note yield and the Nasdaq 100 surged to as much as +0.85.

The Treasury market is regaining its role as a defensive trade.

The correlation between $AAPL and the Nasdaq 100 has now remained negative for 2 consecutive months.

This comes as $AAPL has gained +9.7% over this period, while the Nasdaq 100 has increased just +0.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, the 3-month correlation stood at +0.90, as Apple and other technology stocks rallied together.

To put this into perspective, from 2006 through 2025, the correlation never fell below +0.30.

The divergence between Apple and the rest of the tech sector is unprecedented.

Is China hiding its true exposure to US Treasuries?

China’s Treasury holdings fell -$27 billion in August, to $591 billion, their lowest level since August 2008.

At the same time, Canada’s holdings of US Treasuries jumped +$38 billion in August, to $465 billion, their 3rd-highest on record.

Since the beginning of 2019, Canada’s holdings have surged +$369 billion, or +384%, while China’s have declined -$534 billion, or -48%.

This divergence may partly reflect China moving its US securities to foreign custodians, making its actual exposure to American debt appear smaller and creating the impression of faster financial decoupling from the US Dollar.

Meanwhile, Belgium and Luxembourg, widely believed to hold some Chinese Treasury assets through custodial accounts, increased their Treasury holdings by +$20 billion and +$6 billion in August, to all-time highs of $491 billion and $448 billion, respectively.

China’s diversification away from the US Dollar may be slower than it appears.

Hospitals using AI are seeing better healthcare outcomes.

In 2023, health systems with high and low AI use had the same death rate: ~1,600 per 100,000 patients.

By 2026, the systems using AI the most dropped to ~1,000 deaths per 100,000.

That's a decline of nearly 40% in just 3 years.

Meanwhile, hospitals with lower AI adoption have seen significantly smaller improvements.

The gap in patient outcomes is widening as AI adoption accelerates.

AI is rapidly transforming healthcare.
